title: Short Stuff: The Gaslighting of Martha Mitchell
summary: Short Stuff episode on Martha Mitchell, wife of Nixon's attorney general John Mitchell. Hosts describe her outspoken media habits, her knowledge of the Watergate break-in via James McCord (her former bodyguard, arrested in the break-in), her being held in a hotel and sedated against her will in 1972 on her husband's orders, the Nixon administration's smear campaign portraying her as unstable with a drinking problem, her later testimony for her husband, John Mitchell's prison sentence, her death from cancer in 1976, and the "Martha Mitchell effect" term. They also mention the 2022 series Gaslit starring Julia Roberts.
topics: Committee to Re-elect the President CREEP

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the short episode on Martha Mitchell and describe her as an outspoken, TV-loving political wife in the 1970s.

segments.title: Martha Mitchell's public persona
segments.summary: Hosts describe Martha Mitchell as the 'mouth of the South,' a frequent press talker who was popular with Republicans, including Nixon, and mention the 2022 series Gaslit.

segments.title: John Mitchell and the Watergate break-in
segments.summary: After the June 1972 Watergate break-in, John Mitchell, who had left the attorney general post to head CRP, feared his wife would talk to the press. Her former bodyguard James McCord was among those arrested. The Mitchells were in California when the news broke, and John Mitchell had Martha kept in place away from the press.

segments.title: Why Martha was a threat
segments.summary: Chuck explains that McCord had been assigned as Martha's private bodyguard after John Mitchell left the attorney general role, so her knowledge of McCord's arrest linked her to the campaign. Hosts tease a break.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break and transition back to the episode.

segments.title: Martha held in a hotel and sedated
segments.summary: Martha was kept in a hotel and away from news until she read about the break-in and McCord's arrest. She called reporter Helen Thomas of UPI from a bathroom phone; agent Steve King, per the TV show's depiction, ripped the phone out, and she was tackled and injected with a tranquilizer by a doctor while John Mitchell reassured her by phone.

segments.title: Critique of the hotel operation
segments.summary: Josh criticizes the plan for leaving a phone in her room and suggests a second room; Chuck jokes about hotel newspaper service. They note she was held against her will but not physically injured.

segments.title: Smear campaign and the New York Times story
segments.summary: After her release, Martha went to the press; the New York Times ran the story on page 25. The Nixon administration portrayed her as unstable with a drinking problem, and the press coverage ran in women's pages as gossip.

segments.title: Martha's loyalty, McCord's confirmation, and John Mitchell's cruelty
segments.summary: McCord later confirmed the detention in 1975. Martha called on Nixon to resign, and the campaign intensified its smear. She testified for her husband at his federal trial. John Mitchell made a jab at her after his sentencing of seventeen or eighteen months.

segments.title: Martha Mitchell effect and her death
segments.summary: John Mitchell served about nineteen months after leaving his family in 1973. The term Martha Mitchell effect describes dismissing a justified belief as delusion. Martha died of cancer in 1976. Nixon later said Martha's outcry undermined his denials.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode and Chuck gives the iHeartRadio production credit.
